`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks

pitch:
        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
        as snippets of Piton.

    shape: {ChatInputShape}

shape ChatInputShape:
    description:
        Input on the left, send button on the right.

        The body beneath the tabs has 8 pixels of padding. In it, the text
        input sits in a dark box on the theme's darkest surface, #111111 in
        dark mode, with rounded corners and no border, as tall as the column
        of buttons beside it, 8 pixels from it, and taller when its text
        needs more. The text sits 8 pixels in from the box's top, left, and
        right, and grows down through the box. Clicking anywhere in the box
        beneath the text puts focus in the text, except while a preview
        shows. The preview shows in the same box, its content inset 8 pixels
        all round.

        At the right, a column of three buttons, 120 pixels wide, 6 pixels
        apart, each as tall as the input's single row: Send at the top, then
        Queue, then Preview, each the column's full width. Send has
        a send icon before its label, and keeps its split chevron, the send
        menu staying the only way to reach "Send to task". Queue and Preview
        are buttons in gpui-kit's default style, doing what the
        send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that
        Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that
        Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the
        menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview
        shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also
        disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.

        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}

        Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. While the harness is working, the send
        button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt
        will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is
        never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

    instructions:
    sendOptions:
        splitButton:
            The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself,
            and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a
            menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right
            edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled
            whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its
            tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

        keyboard:
            <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input
            opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing
            while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the
            text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping
            around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes
            the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse
            anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking
            one picks it.

        options:
            The menu's options, in order:
            - "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
            - "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the @{PromptEditor} says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it
            - "Send to task", with a send icon, only while a task is running with a harness that can be fed more, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, and its output is shown, the previous tasks not expanded over it; never on the Ask tab, where a question runs on its own. It sends what is typed, and what is attached, to the running task instead of queueing it, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says, and clears the input as sending does. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) still queues, as the send button does

    tabs:
        overview:
            The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, using
            gpui-kit's default tab styling, except that each tab's label is
            always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, whether selected or not: Code red, Spec blue,
            Ask green, and Freeform grey. There is a tab for each of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and
            Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a
            small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against
            each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a
            normal tab.

            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.

            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
            Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
            not <Cmd>.

            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
            either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

        chain:
            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
            selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its
            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
            is selected.

            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
            them.

            In combined mode, with Chain selected, Chain has no line along its
            bottom, just as the joined Code and Spec beneath it have none. In
            separate mode, unselected, it has one, like any other unselected
            tab: the tab bar's bottom line runs beneath it, the same colour and
            thickness, in the same place, as beneath any other unselected tab,
            at any display scale. This holds at every
            window size and display scale, in light and dark mode: in combined
            mode nothing draws a line beneath Chain at all, rather than a line
            being drawn and then hidden, since a hidden line can show again
            wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.

            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
            Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified
            tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent
            background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec
            show through underneath it.

        help:
            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
        colour:
            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the
            colour of its mode, of the @{PromptModesScope}. With Chain selected,
            Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions
            smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old
            tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing
            <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and
            <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey;
            neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from
            Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling
            its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code
            and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they
            have been given in the theme editor.

            The send button, both its halves, takes the same colour as the
            selected tab, purple with Chain selected, but at full strength
            rather than as a tint, so it stands out against the tinted body.
            Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid
            hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or
            lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part
            them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the
            same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never
            staying solid across a faded button.

    systemPrompt:
    description:
        Beneath the @{RibbonScope}, to the right of the
        @{ProjectSidebarScope}, which runs the full height beside it, and
        reaching the window's right edge. It is part of the @{PromptEditor}.

        The @{ChatInputScope} lives within the body, along its bottom: its
        left edge against the project sidebar, and above it, beneath the
        body's tab bar, the selected tab's contents: the message list, or an
        open file. While a task runs, the @{RightSidebarScope} runs
        the body's full height at its right, beside the tab bar, the selected
        tab's contents, and the chat input, and the chat input's right edge is against it: the chat input
        never runs beneath the right sidebar. While that sidebar isn't there,
        the chat input reaches the window's right edge.

    sliding:

#### Tabs

```
overview: The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it, between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), whether selected or not: Code red, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. The selected tab is marked only by its background, the same surface as the body beneath it, so it reads as a tab joined to that body; unselected tabs have none, and show the strip, lightening a little on hover. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
  The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
  Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
  <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.
chain: Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
  Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
  Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all. Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
  Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
help: To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

I've revamped the body and chat input styling in the spec to match your mockup; the code isn't changed yet. `piton check` finds no problems, formatting is clean, and `piton build` succeeded.

**In `BodyScope`** (`spec/scope/application/Body.pi`): the message list or open file sits on the flat #444444 base grey, edge to edge. The chat input is separated from it only by its darker tab strip.
